paper_title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible fixed-work replay and as inputs to architecture simulators. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments (Yao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). As these tasks grow more complex, multiagent systems (MAS) offer way to divide work among agents with complementary roles. Instead of asking one agent to plan, gather information, act, and verify every step, MAS can organize these activities through specialization, parallel exploration, and iterative feedback. Systems such as AutoGen, MetaGPT, ChatDev, and Magentic-One demonstrate how agents can coordinate their contributions toward shared task (Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Fourney et al., 2024). However, the collaboration that makes MAS useful also reshapes LLM serving demand; its diverse, frameworkspecific patterns hinder reusable workload construction. Conventional serving treats model requests as independent arrivals, while single-agent workflow typically follows one evolving interaction. In MAS, requests may depend on other agents progress and outputs: parallel branches may release several calls together, synchronization may delay down1Peking University. <meng.li@pku.edu.cn>. Correspondence to: Meng Li stream calls, and refinement or debate may trigger repeated exchanges. Agents may inherit histories, share intermediate results, or build new contexts for later calls, changing opportunities for reuse (Bian et al., 2026a;b). Thus, even tasks with similar request counts and token lengths can differ in request readiness, batching opportunities, and memory demand  (Fig. 1)  . These differences arise from task structure, not merely scheduling decisions; request traces record the realized work, not the collaboration rules generating it. Collaboration shapes serving demand in two distinct ways. Work generation determines which model calls, inputs, and token lengths emerge as agents coordinate and exchange results. Work exposure determines when these realized operations become eligible for execution under their dependencies. Legal changes to release constraints can alter batching opportunities and state lifetimes even when the recorded work remains fixed. These effects propagate through execution shapes, weight reuse, and memory demand to completetask latency and deadline attainment. Understanding this chain requires both native workload realizations that capture collaboration-generated work and controlled comparisons that isolate the effects of its legal exposure to serving. Existing work provides complementary perspectives. Multiagent benchmarks evaluate collaboration effectiveness (Chu et al., 2026), while workflow-aware serving optimizes particular mechanisms, such as round-based KV sharing (Bian MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads workloads for architecture simulators. Task-linked hardware evaluation. Functional and replay checks validate the benchmark. GPU/NPU studies connect MAS execution shapes to compute and memory demand, while controlled serving experiments reveal their implications for complete-task SLOs.

sections.title: 2.1 Why Request-Level Workloads Are Insufficient
sections.content: Work generation. Arrival times, input/output lengths, and concurrency describe serving requests, but not the collaboration rules that produce them. Consider research task in which independent agents collect evidence, writer integrates their findings, and reviewer may request revisions. Changing researcher count, revision rounds, or artifact delivery alters calls, contexts, and token work generated, even with shared task bindings and identical root arrivals. Work exposure. At fixed realized work, controlled comparison must identify legal release changes that preserve task semantics. The writer consumes the researchers artifacts, while independent research calls can proceed concurrently. An added barrier may serialize these calls only if it preserves all artifact and state prerequisites and introduces no dependency cycle. Such ordering changes batching opportunities and state lifetimes without altering the recorded work. Selecting only part of research artifact, by contrast, changes the writers resolved input and requires new native realization rather than fixed-work replay. Hardware characterization. Attributing hardware costs to collaboration requires connecting task and stage identities to shared batches, operators, and resources, then locating their effects along task completion paths. Backend scheduling, caching, and placement determine how legally exposed work runs; these system choices must remain distinct from collaboration dependencies.

sections.title: 2.2 Requirements for MAS Hardware Evaluation
sections.content: These gaps motivate four requirements for workload representation, controlled execution, and task-level measurement. R1: Representative Workloads. common workload interface must preserve essential participants, coordination, and context delivery across diverse documented MAS workflows and meaningful tasks. R2: Controllable Collaboration. The benchmark must distinguish native changes to generated work from fixed-work comparisons that vary legal release constraints while preserving recorded requests and their required dependencies. R3: Reproducible Execution. Realized model, tool, transFigure 1. Collaboration reshapes serving demand. (a) Independent request arrivals. (b) multi-agent task induces dependent requests with artifact exchange and synchronization. Both can use continuous batching. (c) MAServeBench enables controlled, reproducible evaluation of collaboration-induced serving demand and hardware resource behavior. et al., 2026b) and dependency-aware scheduling (Wang et al., 2026a; Bian et al., 2026a; Ni et al., 2026). XPerf profiles agentic traces, reconstructs execution graphs, and synthesizes replay workloads by varying arrival patterns (Wang et al., 2026b); AgentSysBench characterizes complete applications (Chang et al., 2026), while AgentPerfBench profiles inference and hardware costs (Lau et al., 2026). MAServeBench instead makes documented collaboration patterns reusable and configurable through composable stages, allowing systems and architecture researchers to construct varied native serving workloads. Semantic Traces then enable legal release comparisons at fixed realized work. We present MAServeBench, benchmark that generates native workloads from configurable collaboration and context rules with identical task inputs and tools. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve each realization for legal release and resource comparisons. Task-linked measurements connect work generation and exposure to serving batches, hardware costs, and complete-task SLOs (Figure 1(c)). We make three contributions: Composable MAS workload construction. We introduce reusable stages capturing agent coordination and context exchange while respecting state dependencies. They compose into MAS workflows whose collaboration rules vary independently of task bindings. Controlled work generation and exposure. Native realizations generate collaboration-dependent work; hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and typed dependencies, enabling controlled fixed-work replay on serving backends and providing MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads formation, and state operations must retain resolved inputs, artifacts, output contracts, and typed dependencies. Replay must preserve this work while leaving target scheduling, batching, and placement decisions free. R4: Hardware Attribution. Measurements must connect task and stage progress to request readiness, batches, operators, and resources. They must distinguish execution opportunities from hardware costs and relate both to complete-task latency and deadline-compliant service.

sections.title: 3.2 Collaboration Stage Semantics
sections.content: Each stage specifies who participates, how they coordinate, and what information they receive: Cs = (Rs, Ctrls, Ctxs). (2) Participants (Rs). Rs specifies participants as logical roles or agent/session slots with input/output interfaces. Roles may be instantiated zero, one, or multiple times according to the stage configuration and control decisions. Execution control (Ctrls). Ctrls governs local activation, concurrency, synchronization, iteration, handoff, and termination through spawn, fork, join, repeat, and finish. Unlike workflow-level composition Γ, these rules coordinate participants within stage. They constrain operation readiness but leave batching, scheduling, and resource management to the serving backend. Context construction (Ctxs). Ctxs selects inherited or fresh history and delivered artifacts or peer outputs, then specifies their ordering and transformation into model inputs. These choices alter generated token work and the opportunities for prefix/KV reuse. Logical memory and state. The workload-level distinguishes private histories, task-shared versioned state, and externally persistent memory when supported. It defines state scope and access rules, while Ctxs selects information for each operation. Versioned reads and writes induce state dependencies; retrieval and compression are explicit operations. Logical state semantics remain distinct from physical KV allocation and eviction.

sections.title: 3.3 Reusable Collaboration Templates
sections.content: The templates share the Rs/Ctrls/Ctxs interface: Spawn. parent activates children with inherited or fresh context and configured return and completion rules. ForkJoin. Independent branches join and aggregate outputs under configurable width and synchronization rules. Refinement Loop. An evaluator provides feedback on an intermediate output, triggering revision until acceptance or configured round limit. Debate. Peers exchange outputs or critiques over bounded rounds, revising responses under configured topology, synchronization, and context rules. Workflows compose these templates and atomic model, tool, or transformation stages through Γ.

sections.title: 4 BENCHMARK DESIGN
sections.content: MAServeBench combines native generation, hierarchical Semantic Traces, and target-side measurement to turn the workload abstraction into controlled serving experiments.

sections.title: 4.1 Benchmark Suite and Workload Construction
sections.content: A task binding supplies inputs, role instructions, tools, and evaluation criteria independently of collaboration rules. The templates in 3 form standalone and composed workflows with configurable control and artifact delivery under shared bindings. Native realization executes collaboration rules and tools to generate concrete operations, inputs, and dependencies. Fixed-work replay preserves those operations, resolved inputs, output contracts, and required dependencies while varying legal release constraints or serving resources. In four-call workflow, two analysts feed synthesis before verification. An optional analyst-to-analyst barrier changes release order while preserving required dependencies. Selecting each analysts answer field instead of its full JSON artifact changes synthesis input through recorded CPU transformation, producing new native realization ( 6.2).

sections.title: 5 VALIDATING MASERVEBENCH
sections.content: We validate MAServeBench at three levels: correspondence to documented collaboration patterns, functional comparability on real tasks, and fidelity of recorded-work replay.

sections.title: 5.1 Source-Grounded Abstraction Validation
sections.content: Structural coverage. Twelve documented workflows cover all four local templates  (Table 3)  ; five compose multiple templates, while MetaGPT uses sequential handoff through Γ. The executable suite exercises seven structures across 30 task bindings, yielding 210 native realizations. separate 21-instance fixed bank, with three bindings per structure, characterizes operation-graph depth, parallel width, and typed dependencies (Appendix A.1). An eight-binding GPT Researcher comparison further examines source-torealization dependency geometry (Appendix A.3). Functional validity. Seven paired native comparisons cover six frameworks and four task sets: SWE-bench Verified, GAIA, WebArena, and DeepResearch Bench. Each pair uses matched task instances, Qwen3.5-9B settings, and evaluation procedures; both the reference workflow and its MAServeBench realization execute natively, allowing generated outputs to determine subsequent work. Quality differences of 1.23.8 percentage points on success/accuracy and at most 0.019 on RACE indicate broadly comparable task outcomes. Comparable task outcomes can still require different model/tool calls and token work, making servingdemand measurement necessary (Appendix A.2).

sections.title: 6 EVALUATION
sections.content: Source-grounded native comparisons assess workflow correspondence; controlled MAS cohorts expose dependency, decoding, and KV regimes, while matched GPU/NPU probes measure hardware sensitivity. Fixed-work interventions isolate release, capacity, and co-execution effects on task latency and goodput. Additional protocols and results appear in the appendix.

The 1k4k range covers 95.898.7% of time-weighted pure-decode context observations in the application controls (Appendix F). KV pressure and task tails. Parallel branches keep agent contexts live concurrently, increasing contention for KV residency. Across three native Qwen3-8B/910C mixed-cohort blocks, 1,372 preemptions amplify processed prefill to 1.76 1.84 source input; Loop-only blocks show neither effect (Figure 9(a)). All preemptions fall in time bins with at least 95% mean KV allocation, linking eviction to costly recomputation of existing contexts. To isolate capacity, 64-root fixed-work replay preserves arrivals, token work, and dependencies across 16/32/40 GiB KV budgets. Greater capacity retains overlapping states, reducing preemptions, redundant prefill, and root P95 in every paired block (b,c). Native traces thus identify collaboration-shaped state pressure; fixed-work controls measure its latency cost, while 6.6 tests release and capacity against task deadlines. Insight 3: Retain overlapping KV states Parallel agents increase concurrent KV residency, turning preemption into costly repeated prefill under memory pressure. At fixed work, expanding KV from 16 to 40 GiB reduces the processed/source prefill factor by 52% and root P95 by 17.5%.

sections.title: 6.6 From Hardware Efficiency to Task SLOs
sections.content: We test how legal release and KV capacity affect task deadlines using 22 DAG/Barrier 16/40 GiB comparison for SpawnForkJoinRefinement on Qwen3-8B/910C. Barrier adds three ordering edges among four independent analyses. Across four arrival rates and three paired blocks, recorded work, required dependencies, and Poisson arrivals remain fixed. The shared 361.7-second deadline is 1.5 an independent low-load DAG/40 GiB reference P95. Task goodput counts timely roots, including drain completions, per arrivalwindow duration; output TPS uses drain-inclusive duration. Release constraints affect task completion even without KV recomputation. The first three rates incur no KV preemption, yet at the second rate DAG achieves 100% median deadline attainment versus Barriers 4% under either KV budget (Figure 12). Improved hardware efficiency does not guarantee better task SLOs. At the highest rate, 40 GiB eliminates preemption observed at 16 GiB in two blocks per release rule, reducing DAG root P95 by 15.5% and increasing output TPS by 7.7%. Nevertheless, deadline goodput remains near zero: these execution savMAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads bate repeatedly release dependent calls. Phase specialization must offset KV/state-transfer costs and cross-pool queueing, especially for long contexts and hybrid-model recurrent state. Replay extensions that associate phase placement and state transfers with each operation could evaluate these designs through complete-task SLOs.

sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multi-agent frameworks and collaboration evaluation. AutoGen, MetaGPT, ChatDev, and Magentic-One implement collaborative workflows (Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Fourney et al., 2024); AgentBench and MultiAgentBench evaluate agent outcomes and coordination (Liu et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). These works motivate representative collaboration patterns, whereas MAServeBench examines how altering those patterns changes serving demand and task performance. Agentic serving and hardware benchmarking. XPerf profiles observed agentic traces, reconstructs execution graphs, and synthesizes serving workloads by varying graph arrivals for DAG-aware, token-wise replay (Wang et al., 2026b). AgentReplay studies token-wise fidelity and optional router replay (Pan et al., 2026). AgentSysBench characterizes complete applications while varying orchestration and deployment factors (Chang et al., 2026), while AgentPerfBench profiles agentic inference and kernel costs (Lau et al., 2026). Maestro, TokenCake, and TokenDance exploit workflow or context structure for serving (Wang et al., 2026a; Bian et al., 2026a;b); Chakra standardizes execution traces (Sridharan et al., 2026). MAServeBench instead makes collaboration semantics workload-generation variable: shared task bindings reveal changes in calls, contexts, and typed dependencies, while hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve each realization for release and resource controls linked to serving, hardware, and task-SLO measurements.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: MAServeBench provides source-grounded, extensible benchmark for multi-agent serving. Composable stages vary collaboration and context construction under shared task bindings, generating distinct workloads through native execution. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for controlled comparisons of legal release and serving resources at fixed work. Tasklinked measurements reveal how collaboration shapes parallelism, locality affects compute efficiency, and KV pressure impacts task completion. Decoupling workflow semantics from backend execution lets Semantic Traces serve as workloads for serving backends and architecture simulators, supporting MAS serving and hardware evaluation. sections.title: 6.7 Discussion
sections.content: Reuse-aware compute and tiered KV memory. The GPU reversal motivates SRAM/L2 retention for reusable weights and cache bypass with HBM streaming for rotating weights; Gather motivates programmable SIMT with access-aware path selection. page-managed HBM pool could asynchronously extend KV into DRAM when migration and remote access cost less than saved prefill. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) could hold cold, read-mostly weights with low update traffic; 3D near-memory attention could benefit long contexts when saved data movement exceeds transfer overhead. These hypotheses must advance timely task completion; dependency hints and input-prefix reuse could guide retention and prefetch. Multi-replica and disaggregated serving. Consider production MAS whose agents invoke model APIs backed by replicas across machines or clusters. Prefix affinity can save prefill but concentrate demand on contended replica, making routing and load balancing affect complete-task latency and SLOs even with fixed dependencies. MAServeBench separates logical collaboration from physical placement; an API-facing replay adapter could preserve recorded work and arrivals while exposing per-replica routing and queueing, including delays before submission.
